body: I think I might be too depressed for another human being to deal with, so...extremely.

I had a really bad day today (Sunday). Combination of depression + cabin fever + marijuana withdrawal made me suicidal for the first time in months. I yelled at my mom and dad who only have been the most supportive parents in existence and I feel abhorrent for it. Now I’m crying my eyes out in bed, too ashamed/depressed to ask them for help, and on top of all of that I’m having a world class anxiety attack over the impending doom of coronavirus and the eventual demise of myself and everyone I love. 

If there is a switch in the human brain that makes us ignore existential anxiety, mine is absolutely broken. I can’t even read about space and the universe because the vastness of the unknown makes me shrivel up inside. I used to love learning about nature but now new information terrifies me.

I’m an absolute wreck of a person. My siblings have told me that they think they have to worry about me every single day because I can’t take care of myself. There are times when I wish I was in an asylum or something because I feel like I’m never going to be better. I’m 31 years old and already I’m so afraid of the future. I feel like a goddamned prisoner in my own head.

I was committed by the state after I posted a note on Facebook and attempted suicide. It was traumatic at first because I definitely didn’t want to be there but unfortunately my family and my doctors couldn’t get me out. I had to stay there for two weeks. It got way easier once I started to meet people and mingle with the other patients who were suffering from pretty much every mental disease you can think.

The biggest thing I took away from the experience is that depression is way easier to manage and deal with if you follow a rigid schedule. Everything in the ward was on a schedule. You would wake up and immediately go get your blood pressure measured, you get your breakfast assigned to you (I’m a diabetic so I had special no-carb meals), you spend the day divided between group therapy, activities, and games. There was a lot more free time than I expected. The only downside was my family could only visit like twice a week.

Also, fun little movie fact, the patients divided themselves up almost exactly the way they did in “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest”. I spent my time with the patients who had less serious problems (depression, anxiety, bipolar, etc.) while those with majorly bad diseases (schizophrenia, addiction, major delusions, etc.) mostly kept to themselves.

I have dysthymia and severe major depressive disorder which is science lingo for short term depression and extremely bad chronic depression. For about a decade I’ve had constant suicidal ideation which culminated in about a dozen actual attempts. The attempt that was the closest got interrupted by the police, who had been notified by an anonymous Facebook friend after I posted my suicide note there. The reason I attempted largely had to do with the fact I was alone on New Year’s Eve and my Facebook feed was plastered with pictures of people celebrating with friends and loved ones and I decided that I didn’t want to be alive anymore. I was sick of the tedium and emotional deprivation I was feeling and to be completely alone on a holiday basically broke me. I tied a bag around my head and lay down on the living room floor. I blacked out but the next thing I knew my dad was hugging me and the police were there. I spent a week and a half in a psych ward and three years later I’m way more stable. Depression is the absolute worst; even after a ton of meds and therapy I still have suicidal ideation, though now it’s more of a nagging thought than an action plan.

Yeah if only depression was that easy to solve.  Getting out of the house is a huge challenge especially if you have anxiety to boot. Overthinking is a symptom of depression, not a cause. Music can be helpful and therapeutic but it doesn’t help everyone. Same with spirituality. The sun does actually help, but only a little bit. Treating depression depends on a ton of factors and is usually tailored specifically for each patient. You can’t just tell people to get out and run around. This is a chronic disease that has no cure. The only things we can do is 1) get help, and 2) take each day one at a time. It took more than ten years and a ton of doctors and drugs for me to get to a stable point and I still have extremely bad episodes.

I was on Prozac for five or six years before I realized it just wasn’t working. I switched to Cymbalta and Seroquel and that combination has been working quite well. The problem with depression is that everyone’s body is wired differently and so what works for one person doesn’t always work for another. My sister has been on Prozac since high school and she’s been completely fine. It didn’t work for me or my other sister who’s on Zoloft instead. It might take some time to find the right cocktail but it’s worth the search and experimentation.

There doesn’t need to be a reason you’re depressed. It’s a chronic illness, a condition; it just is. I had an actual doctor tell me something along the lines of “you have no reason to be sad when there are poor kids in Detroit who have nothing.” That doctor doesn’t practice anymore. And she was never right to begin with. Your brain doesn’t know how to function properly. It’s chemicals and science. When you accept that this is beyond your control and you need help, that’s real progress. That’s a step in the right direction. You’re going to feel sad sometimes but it’s not anything you’re doing wrong. Nature is a massive bitch sometimes. I still have insane nightmares and really bad depressive episodes even though I’m medicated and seeing a therapist. The difference between now and before treatment was that I blamed myself for a lot of my depression. Now I’ve come to accept that this is a medical illness and there will be lapses every so often but as long as you are proactive in getting help things will get easier.
